blocks.text: ==95%== of women have mild **PMS** symptoms; ==5%== suffer severe symptoms; severe **PMS** affects 3-==8%== of women of reproductive age. Comorbidity with a mood disorder is seen in 30-==70%==; **PMDD** carries a higher risk of postnatal depression.

**PMDD** (**DSM-5**) requires ≥5 of 11 symptoms (including ≥1 of depressed mood/marked anxiety/marked affective lability/marked anger-irritability) present in most cycles over the past year, confined to the last week of the luteal phase, remitting within days of menses onset, confirmed by prospective daily ratings over ≥2 cycles. Breast tenderness/bloating are not seen in major depressive disorder and help distinguish **PMDD**.

blocks.text: Aetiology: increased sensitivity to normal gonadal-hormone fluctuation (not a drop in progesterone). Serotonin has a pathogenic role; **GABA-A**/progesterone-metabolite interaction is also implicated.

SSRIs (**fluoxetine** most studied/most effective, also **sertraline**, **citalopram**, **escitalopram**, **clomipramine**, **venlafaxine**) have a 60-==90%== response rate vs 30-==40%== placebo (Dimmock 2000 meta-analysis **OR** 6.91). Effects appear within one cycle - too rapid to be a classic antidepressant mechanism.

Intermittent luteal-phase dosing is effective only during the 2 weeks pre-menses, is cheaper, has fewer withdrawal effects, and is more effective than continuous/semi-continuous dosing (Wikander 1998) for core symptoms, though less effective than continuous dosing for somatic symptoms. No significant difference between continuous and intermittent dosing overall (Dimmock 2000).

**SSRI** in **PMS** differs from **SSRI** in depression: low (not high) frequency of sexual side effects, intermittent (not continuous) dosing more effective, effective within days (not 3-4 weeks), no reported akathisia/increased suicidal ideation.

blocks.text: ==20%== of coronary heart disease patients have comorbid depression (Ramamurthy 2013). Psychological/behavioural interventions reduce depression and mortality in **CAD** (Welton 2009); persistent depression despite treatment raises cardiac risk (**OR** 1.53, Nicholson 2006).

**SADHART** (**sertraline** vs placebo, 16 weeks, post-**MI** depression) showed no safety difference (**LVEF**, PVCs, QTc) and a nonsignificant reduction in **MI**/**CHD** death with **sertraline** (**RR** 0.77, ==95%== **CI** 0.51-1.16), suggesting possible cardioprotection via reduced platelet activation; benefit was greater in severe/recurrent depression.
**ENRICHD** (**CBT**) and **MIND-IT** trials had only modest effects on depression and neither improved survival.

Depression prevalence in **CHF** is ~==21.5%== (~==19%== meet formal **MDD** criteria) - about 2-3x (risk ratio 3:1) the general-population rate; similar in inpatients and outpatients, higher with higher **NYHA** class and in women. Relative mortality risk in depressed **CHF** patients is ~2:1 vs non-depressed **CHF** patients.

Depression risk in **CHF** versus the general population is quoted as an exact 3:1 ratio (==21.5%== prevalence) - option lists offer nearby-sounding wrong ratios (1:8, 5:1, 1:7, 1:5) to test precise recall.

blocks.text: Hyperthyroidism: most commonly generalized anxiety; also depression, irritability, hypomania, cognitive dysfunction; mania can occur in severe thyrotoxicosis. Hypothyroidism: M:F ratio 1:6; depression often misdiagnosed as primary **MDD**, myxoedema madness (psychosis) in severe cases; subclinical hypothyroidism is a risk factor for depression and for rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

Hyperparathyroidism symptoms track serum calcium: mild-moderate (10-14 mg/dL) causes depression/apathy/irritability; severe (>14 mg/dL) causes delirium with psychosis, catatonia, or lethargy progressing to coma. Hypoparathyroidism: mild hypocalcaemia causes anxiety/paraesthesias/irritability/lability; severe causes mania, psychosis, tetany, seizures.

Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess, most commonly exogenous steroids; pituitary source = Cushing's disease): psychiatric symptoms may precede physical signs; depression is the most common symptom, followed by anxiety, hypomania/mania, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction. Exogenous steroids produce more mania than endogenous excess; effects are often dose-related.

Addison's disease (cortisol depletion): apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, depressed mood (may mimic primary **MDD**) - but nausea, vomiting, and skin pigmentation changes point to Addison's rather than depression.

Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumour): episodic tachycardia, labile hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations that can mimic panic attacks. Screen with urinary catecholamines (**VMA**, metanephrines); the best diagnostic test is a plasma metanephrine level (more specific).

Depression is 2-3x more common in diabetics than the general population and is linked to poorer glycaemic control and more complications. Type 2 diabetes prevalence is 2-4x higher in bipolar disorder/schizophrenia/severe depression. Recurrent hypoglycaemia rarely causes permanent cognitive dysfunction; frequent hyperglycaemia causing cerebral micro/macrovascular damage is the more common route to cognitive impairment.
Subclinical hypothyroidism (not hyper/hypoparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, or hypopituitarism) is the specific risk factor tested for both depression and rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

sections.title: 4. Renal Medicine: Psychotropic Prescribing & Uraemic Syndromes

blocks.text: **Diazepam**'s half-life is unchanged in end-stage renal disease but its metabolite desmethyldiazepam accumulates. **Lorazepam**'s half-life rises from 8-25h (normal) to 32-72h in end-stage renal disease; reduce dose by ==50%== at low renal function to avoid excessive sedation.

**Imipramine**/**amitriptyline**: usual dosage in renal impairment (half-life unaffected). **Citalopram**: half the normal dose in renal impairment/elderly. **Paroxetine** half-life is considerably increased in severe renal impairment (reduce dose). **Fluoxetine**/**fluvoxamine**: no dose reduction needed in elderly or renal impairment. **Sertraline**: manufacturer does not recommend use in renal impairment.

**Haloperidol** needs no dose reduction in renal impairment unless sedation/hypotension occur. **Amisulpride** is almost exclusively renally excreted, so renal failure is a relative contraindication (alternate-day dosing/dose reduction if no alternative). **Risperidone** and its active metabolite are substantially renally excreted, prolonging elimination half-life in renal impairment. **Lithium** is best avoided or used at low dose in renal impairment.

blocks.text: Uraemic encephalopathy occurs when **GFR** falls to ==10%== of normal; onset rate tracks the rate of **GFR** decline; causes cognitive/psychomotor/personality change with vomiting, restlessness, myoclonus, coma - reversible with dialysis, transplant, or treating the underlying disease.

Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome occurs during/after early dialysis sessions, more common in younger patients and those with pre-existing neurological problems (cerebral trauma, recent stroke); mild symptoms (headache, restlessness) can progress to nausea, vomiting, hypertension, tremor, disorientation, seizures - mostly secondary to cerebral oedema. Now less common with improved dialysis technology.

blocks.text: Major depression prevalence in advanced cancer is 5-==15%== (another 10-==15%== have less severe symptoms). Somatic symptoms are not useful for diagnosing depression here; pervasive global anhedonia is the more useful criterion.

**SSRI** evidence in palliative depression is limited/not well established; low-dose **amitriptyline** is useful if neuropathic pain is present but should be avoided in those at higher delirium risk; **lofepramine** and rapid-acting psychostimulants (dexamphetamine, **methylphenidate**) are useful, particularly for patients with only weeks of life.

Delirium prevalence in cancer inpatients is ~==44%==, rising to ==62%== shortly before death; aetiology is usually multifactorial and a specific cause is found in <==50%== of terminally ill patients. Low-dose **haloperidol** or **lorazepam** is frequently used but not always successful, especially in the hypoactive (sedated) subtype.

**SSRI** evidence for depression in palliative care is described as feeble/largely empirical - the exam marks "**SSRI** evidence here is well established" as the false statement, contrasted with **amitriptyline** (neuropathic pain but delirium risk), **lorazepam** (acute anxiety), and **risperidone** (psychotic symptoms).

sections.title: 6. Other Medical Disorders with Neuropsychiatric Presentations

blocks.text: Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi via tick bite): erythema migrans develops within 4 weeks; ~==15%== develop neuroborreliosis (rare in **UK**, more common in North America) with back pain worse at night, facial numbness/palsy. Late-stage disease can cause memory impairment, word-finding problems, psychosis, seizures, violent behaviour, anxiety, depression - can mimic any encephalopathy/psychiatric disorder, often compared to neurosyphilis.

**SLE**: nonorgan-specific vasculitis with antinuclear antibodies; butterfly rash, joint/kidney/serosal injury. Depression and anxiety common, particularly early after diagnosis and with disfiguring skin lesions; psychosis is rare. **CNS** manifestations include peripheral neuropathy (rarely Guillain-Barre), grand mal seizures, chorea, cognitive impairment, severe headache, stroke, B-cell lymphoma, and a limbic-encephalitis-type picture.

Insulinoma (a common pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour) can present with neuropsychiatric symptoms often misdiagnosed as psychosis/depression; classically recurrent headache, lethargy, diplopia and blurred vision, particularly with exercise or fasting.

Neurosarcoidosis: idiopathic granulomas (mainly lung/mediastinal nodes) that can affect cranial nerves (bilateral facial palsy); depression in ==20%==, psychosis rare; erythema nodosum on the shin is a cutaneous sign; **ACE** levels elevated from macrophage activity; treated with immunosuppression.

Metachromatic leucodystrophy (arylsulfatase A deficiency) has infantile, juvenile, and adult forms; nearly ==60%== of adolescent-onset cases have schizophrenia-like psychosis (not seen in younger-onset cases); the adult form commonly begins after age 16 as a psychiatric disorder or progressive dementia.

Neuroacanthocytosis: movement disorder/ataxia with personality change (impulsivity, distractibility, anxiety, depression, apathy), cognitive deterioration, axonal neuropathy, seizures; acanthocytosis affects typically 10-==30%== of erythrocytes; subcortical dementia may develop.

blocks.text: Onset age 20-40; **UK** lifetime risk 1:8000; twice as common in women; incidence rises with distance from the equator. Predominantly white-matter disease with plaques in optic nerves, cerebellum, brain stem, spinal cord. 5-==10%== primary progressive (no remission); 20-==30%== relapsing-remitting without serious disability; ==60%== secondary progressive after relapses/remissions.

Depression lifetime prevalence 40-==50%== (~3x general population), linked to poorer cognitive function, poor treatment compliance, lower quality of life. Drug-induced low mood is an important differential: steroids (more likely), baclofen, dantrolene, tizanidine. Interferon-**ALPHA** (used in viral hepatitis) - not beta-interferon - is the one clearly linked to depression; the beta-interferon association is controversial/contested.

Desipramine and SSRIs have an evidence base for **MS** depression. **ECT** may be used but carries a ==20%== risk of triggering an **MS** relapse; active **MRI** lesions before treatment are a risk factor for relapse post-**ECT** - **ECT** is not absolutely contraindicated. Suicide accounts for ==3%== of **MS** deaths over 6 years and ==15%== over 16 years; suicidal ideation is present cross-sectionally in nearly ==30%==.

Mania: higher-than-expected prevalence, can be drug-induced (steroids more likely than baclofen/dantrolene/tizanidine). Mild-to-moderate mania occurs in up to 1/3rd (not 2/3rd) of steroid-treated patients; steroid-induced hypomania is linked to family/premorbid affective disorder and/or alcoholism history.
**MRI** evidence shows mania-with-psychotic-symptoms plaques distributed predominantly in the bilateral **TEMPORAL** **HORN** areas (not a frontal distribution).

Pathological laughing/crying (emotionalism/pseudobulbar affect): mood-incongruent, involuntary; ==66%== of **MS** patients responded to **amitriptyline** 75mg/day in one study; amantadine, **levodopa**, **fluoxetine**, **sertraline**, and **citalopram** have also shown benefit.

blocks.text: Mean duration of post-stroke major depression is 34 weeks. Left-hemisphere-lesion depressogenicity has been contested recently; major depression is common with infarcts involving the basal ganglia, especially on the left.

blocks.text: Symptom prevalences in epilepsy (Dilley & Fleminger 2006): depression 30-==50%==, panic disorder ==20%==, psychosis 3-==7%==. Depression is associated with stigma/demoralization and is especially common in temporal lobe epilepsy. Suicide risk is high even without depression (10-==15%== in some cohorts); mortality is nearly 25x higher when clinical depression is present.

SSRIs are first-line for depression in epilepsy (rare seizure-threshold reduction); **lithium** can increase seizure severity and reduce seizure threshold. Panic attacks can be interictal or periictal and must be differentiated from seizure activity.

Psychosis is more common in partial epilepsies; episodic psychosis is most often post-ictal (visual hallucinations more common than in functional psychosis). Antiepileptic-drug-related psychosis lasts <1 week; **vigabatrin** is especially associated with psychosis. **Sulpiride** and **haloperidol** may be less epileptogenic than other antipsychotics.

Pseudoseizures (non-epileptic seizures) associate with past psychiatric history, somatisation, and social stressors (esp. childhood abuse); more likely daytime and with others present; side-to-side head movement, tightly shut eyes (vs open eyes in true seizures), preserved body tone, rapid alertness/orientation recovery, and clear event recall. Incontinence has no diagnostic value; an abnormal **EEG** does not always mean epilepsy. Increased postictal serum prolactin (>1000 **IU**/l) supports true epilepsy but must be measured within 15 minutes.

blocks.title: Psychiatric manifestations of Parkinson's disease (Dilley & Fleminger, 2006)

blocks.text: Depression risk factors: female gender, younger onset, prominent right-sided lesions, bradykinesia/gait disturbance, rapid disease progression, poorer cognitive status/ADLs. Apathy without depression is common and linked to executive dysfunction, and may be masked by Parkinsonian affect.

De novo mania is rare in **PD**; mania is mostly related to **levodopa**/dopamine-agonist treatment, especially with pre-existing bipolar disorder or family history. **Levodopa** can also cause pathological gambling, hypersexuality, and hallucinations. Psychosis is mostly drug-related (dopaminergic and anticholinergic); visual hallucinations occur in ==20%==, delusions in 3-==30%==.

Low-dose **clozapine** (<100mg/day) can improve psychosis without worsening Parkinsonism; **quetiapine** can also be used. Cognitive impairment risk factors: older age, late-onset **PD**, low socioeconomic status/education, severe extrapyramidal signs. Frontal-executive dysfunction with a subcortical dementia pattern is typical; Lewy body dementia is pathologically closely related and **rivastigmine** is useful there; no drug is yet licensed for **PD**-related dementia.

Cognitive-impairment risk factors are older age, **LATE**-onset **PD**, **LOW** socioeconomic status, **LOW** education, and severe extrapyramidal signs - younger age, early onset, high **SES**, and fewer extrapyramidal signs are the deliberate false-option pairings.

sections.title: 12. Wilson's Disease, Fahr's Disease & Meige Syndrome

blocks.text: Wilson's disease: exclusively psychiatric presentation in ==20%== of cases; ==50%== have mental disturbance at some point (personality change, mood abnormality, cognitive dysfunction most common); psychiatric manifestations occur more with neurological than hepatic forms. Cognitive impairment in up to ==25%== (frontosubcortical pattern); depression in ==30%==; suicidal behaviour in 4-==16%==; psychosis is rare (~==2%==) but can be the initial presentation (Ring & Serra-Mestres 2002).

Kayser-Fleischer rings (corneal copper deposits) are present in ==95%== of patients with neurological symptoms, 50-==60%== without neurological symptoms, and only ==10%== of asymptomatic siblings. **MRI** can show the "giant panda sign" (midbrain hyperintensity sparing the red nucleus/superior colliculus/part of the substantia nigra, with aqueduct hypointensity). Copper-chelating/depleting treatment can improve most manifestations if started early.

blocks.title: Kayser-Fleischer ring prevalence in Wilson's disease by patient group

blocks.text: Fahr's disease: idiopathic basal-ganglia calcium deposition; onset 20-40 years old associates with schizophreniform psychosis/catatonic symptoms, while onset 40-60 associates with dementia and choreoathetosis. ==50%== have psychiatric problems, correlating with more extensive calcification; depression common, mania much less so; frontosubcortical cognitive pattern. Radiological calcification without clinical features occurs at ~==0.9%== on **CT**; **MRI** shows striatal hypointensity; **EEG** is non-specific.

Meige syndrome (oral facial dystonia, repetitive blinking and chin thrusting, first described by Henri Meige 1904): more common in women, usually middle age; primary form is idiopathic, secondary form caused by antipsychotics, **levodopa**, or Lewy body dementia. Present both at rest and when active; disappears with sleep.
Meige syndrome is more common in **WOMEN**, not men - the option asking "which statement is incorrect" marks the male-predominance claim as the false one.

blocks.text: The most common cause of viral and limbic encephalitis, affecting temporal lobe/limbic circuit; ==70%== caused by **HSV-1** (immunocompromised patients may have **HSV-2**, **HHV-6**/7). blocks.text: Peak incidence of head injury is age 15-24. Concussion causes transient coma followed by apparent recovery; contusion causes prolonged coma, focal signs, lasting damage - though pathological support for this division is poor. **TBI** mechanisms: shearing/rotational stress (contrecoup), direct trauma, oedema/raised **ICP**, hypoxia/ischaemia.

Post-traumatic amnesia (**PTA**, anterograde, from injury until normal memory resumes) durations map to severity/outcome: <60min = mild (return to work <1 month); 1-24h = moderate (<2 months); 1-7 days = severe (<4 months); >7 days = very severe (>1 year). Retrograde amnesia (dense amnesia before injury) generally reduces over minutes.

blocks.text: Poor psychiatric-morbidity prognostic factors: long **LOC**/**PTA**, elderly, chronic alcohol use, diffuse brain damage, new-onset seizures, focal damage to the **DOMINANT** lobe. **LOC**/**PTA** are more predictive of functional outcome than **GCS**; **AIS** predicts survival.

Depression is the most common late sequela (with anxiety, roughly 1/4 of survivors); left-frontal lesion proximity predicts depression. Schizophrenia-like psychosis with prominent paranoia links to left temporal injury; affective psychosis (mania in ==9%==) links to right temporal/orbitofrontal injury. Schizophrenia incidence increases post-head-injury (~==2.5%== develop it). Post-traumatic epilepsy occurs in ==5%== of closed and ==30%== of open injuries, usually in year one, worsening prognosis. Children show less psychopathology due to greater brain plasticity.

Post-concussion syndrome follows mild (**PTA**<1h, **GCS** 13-15, **LOC**<15min) or moderate (**PTA** 1-24h, **GCS** 9-12, **LOC** 15min-6h) head injury; symptoms include headache, dizziness, fatigue, poor memory/concentration, irritability, depression, sleep disturbance, photophobia, tinnitus. At least ==50%== recover fully within 3 months; slower recovery with age >40, prior head injury, or alcohol/substance misuse. Early intervention (a single hour-long assessment/treatment session with education plus reassurance) significantly reduces persisting symptoms.
Poor prognosis after head injury is linked to focal damage of the **DOMINANT** lobe - damage to the non-dominant lobe is deliberately offered as the incorrect "except" answer.

blocks.text: **ICSD** divides dyssomnias (primary insomnia/hypersomnia, circadian sleep disorders, narcolepsy, breathing-related disorders, sleep-state misperception) from parasomnias, subdivided by sleep phase: **NREM** arousal disorders (confusional arousals, sleepwalking, sleep terrors), sleep-wake transition disorders (sleep starts, sleep talking), and **REM** parasomnias (**REM** behavioural disorder, nightmares, sleep paralysis). Other parasomnias include bruxism and enuresis.

Delayed sleep phase syndrome (most common circadian disorder): inability to fall asleep until very early morning, progressively delaying over time. Narcolepsy: prevalence ==0.025%==; excessive daytime sleepiness/sleep attacks, cataplexy (==75%==), sleep paralysis (==30%==), hypnagogic hallucinations (only ==10%== have all four features); associated with **HLA-DQB1*0602** and low **CSF** hypocretin-1 (orexin-A); sleep polysomnogram shows sleep latency <10 min with sleep-onset **REM**. Stimulants (**methylphenidate**, **modafinil**) treat sleepiness; **imipramine** may help cataplexy.

Obstructive sleep apnoea more common in men (==4%==) than women (==2.5%==); snoring is the most common presenting symptom; untreated cases risk right-sided cardiac failure. Sleepwalking arises from slow-wave (stage 3/4) sleep, mostly in the first third of the night; sleep terrors similarly occur in stages 3/4 **NREM** in the first third of the night, with panicky screaming, no recall, and unresponsiveness during the episode.

**REM** sleep behaviour disorder: loss of normal **REM** atonia, dreams acted out (sometimes violently); occurs in the middle-to-latter third of the night; may be idiopathic or prodromal to Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy, Guillain-Barre syndrome (associated lesions likely in the brainstem). **Clonazepam** is effective treatment; making the sleep environment safe is first-line.

Restless legs syndrome (age ≥12): akathisia-like urge to move legs (core feature) with paraesthesias, motor restlessness, symptoms worse at rest and at night; an awake phenomenon; prevalence 3-==15%== (median ==7.2%==), M:F 1:2, familial pattern in >==50%== of primary cases. Predisposing factors include iron deficiency (check ferritin/iron saturation), peripheral neuropathy, sedating antihistamines, dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), antipsychotics, caffeine, most antidepressants (except **bupropion**). Treatment: sleep hygiene, non-ergot dopamine agonists (**ropinirole** - first licensed - **pramipexole**), anticonvulsants (**gabapentin**, **carbamazepine**), opioids, **clonazepam**; oral iron if ferritin low.

Periodic limb movement disorder is an **ASLEEP** phenomenon (contrast with **RLS**, an awake phenomenon), diagnosed by polysomnography; **PLMS** occur in up to ==34%== of people over 60, and are common in **RLS** (80-==90%==), narcolepsy (45-==65%==), and **REM** behaviour disorder (==70%==); dopaminergic impairment and iron deficiency implicated, as in **RLS**. Pharmacological treatment is not warranted unless there is clear sleep disruption.

Periodic limb movement disorder is an **ASLEEP** phenomenon, unlike restless legs syndrome which is an **AWAKE** phenomenon - the two conditions are repeatedly contrasted and their awake/asleep labels swapped as distractors.

blocks.text: **CFS** prevalence: **US** community samples 0.23-==0.42%==, **UK** sample ==2.6%== falling to ==0.5%== after excluding comorbid psychological disease. Higher in women (M:F 1:3), lower occupational/educational status; mean onset age 29-35; mean duration 3-9 years; lower prevalence but still diagnosed in children/adolescents.

**US** **CDC** (1994) criteria: persistent/relapsing unexplained chronic fatigue of new onset lasting ≥6 months, not explained by organic disease or continuing exertion, not relieved by rest, plus ≥4 of: impaired memory/concentration, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, muscle pain, multi-joint pain, new headaches, unrefreshing sleep, post-exertional malaise. Excludes major psychiatric disorders (psychotic depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, dementia, eating disorders, substance misuse) - but non-psychotic psychiatric disorders are **NOT** exclusion criteria.

Predictors of poor outcome (Powell 2004): claiming disability benefit, low sense of control, strong focus on physical symptoms, passivity with reduced activity, self-help group membership (an indicator of perceived severity, not a cause). Severity and duration of illness are **NOT** useful predictors of treatment response.

==33%== of **CFS** patients are unable to work, ==33%== work only part-time. **NICE** red-flag symptoms suggesting an alternative serious illness: significant weight loss, significant lymphadenopathy, focal neurological signs, inflammatory arthritis/connective tissue/cardiorespiratory disease features, sleep apnoea.

Aetiology is multifactorial: predisposing (neuroticism, childhood inactivity/illness), precipitating (infectious mononucleosis, Q fever, Lyme disease, life events), perpetuating (belief in physical cause, activity avoidance, poor self-control, primary/secondary gain, low self-perceived cognitive ability). **HPA**-axis and serotonin-pathway abnormality is the most consistent finding; 1/3 have hypocortisolism of **CNS** (not primary adrenal) origin; family studies suggest cortisol-transporting-globulin mutation.

**CBT** and graded exercise therapy are the only evidence-based treatments; **CBT** is not a cure but its effect can last up to 5 years in responders (Deale 2001) by targeting cognitive/behavioural drivers (misperceived cause, activity avoidance, excessive rest). Medication added to **CBT** improved outcomes, but **CBT** added to medication did not - timing matters (Stubhaug 2008).

**CBT** vs graded exercise therapy (**GET**): **CBT** is behavioural/avoidance-model-based, always includes graded activity, ~==70%== improvement, more complex training; **GET** is deconditioning-model-based, doesn't specifically treat cognition (though some studies add cognitive work), ~==55%== improvement, less complex training. Antidepressants should not be used routinely in **CFS**; if used, severity-guided, mindful that prolonged inactivity raises autonomic side-effect risk and sedation can worsen fatigue.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** replaced pain disorder/somatization disorder/hypochondriasis/undifferentiated somatoform disorder with Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders (**SSD**) - diagnosed on **POSITIVE** symptoms/signs (distressing somatic symptoms plus abnormal thoughts/feelings/behaviours), not on absence of a medical explanation.

Pain is the most common presenting somatic symptom in medical outpatients; depression occurs in 10-==15%== of pain-disorder patients (also common: substance misuse, **PTSD**, Geisser 1996); ==43%== of depressed adults report pain (Ohayon & Schatzberg 2003). Treatments improving depression give moderate reductions in pain severity/disability via a shared central pain-modulation mechanism. **CBT** for chronic pain works best with cognitive restructuring, relaxation training, time-based activity pacing, and graded homework against avoidance.

Atypical/persistent idiopathic facial pain (Frazier & Russell 1924; **IHS** 2004 criteria): unilateral, poorly localised, present most of the day, described as severe ache/crushing/burning, not fitting any cranial neuralgia, no sensory loss or imaging/lab abnormality. Depression and anxiety are prevalent; treatment requires a difficult multidisciplinary approach.

**BAP** guidelines (Cleare 2015): there is a lack of compelling evidence that SNRIs are more effective than SSRIs for pain symptoms associated with depression, and no clinically useful predictive biological factor for antidepressant response has been identified.

blocks.text: **HIV**-associated acute stress reaction typically occurs on informing someone of seropositivity or transition to full **AIDS** - brooding about the future, panic attacks, social isolation, rage, or desperation appearing within minutes-to-hours and remitting within 2-3 days.

Adjustment disorder with anxiety/depressed mood occurs in 5-==20%== of **HIV**-infected patients. Anxiety symptoms/disorders occur in 11-==25%==; "worried well" describes seronegative high-risk individuals whose anxiety about infection can progress to **GAD**, panic disorder, **OCD**, or hypochondriasis despite repeated negative tests.

Depression is the most common **HIV** psychiatric disorder - ~==40%== (30-==60%== lifetime), higher in women, and became the most common cause of psychiatric hospitalisation in some countries post-**HAART**. High-risk groups for **HIV** (**STD** history, homosexual men, lower socioeconomic groups) also independently carry higher depression risk; some depression criteria (poor sleep, weight loss) overlap with **HIV** symptoms, spuriously inflating rates. Suicide risk factors include **AIDS**-related bereavement, recent seropositivity notification, relapse, social difficulties around homosexuality, poor support, and comorbid dementia/delirium.

TCAs and SSRIs are equally effective for **HIV** depression; SSRIs are safer in overdose with fewer side effects and can be started at ==25%== of the usual dose. Secondary-amine TCAs (desipramine, **nortriptyline**) are preferred, reserved for asymptomatic illness; **AIDS** patients respond to lower **TCA** doses (25-100mg) but may still get severe anticholinergic effects. Interpersonal psychotherapy is particularly beneficial; combining psychotherapy with medication may be optimal (Markowitz).

Psychotic symptoms are usually late-stage, uncommon, and may reflect direct neurotoxicity, iatrogenic causes, or substance misuse. **AIDS** patients on typical antipsychotics are particularly prone to extrapyramidal side effects and **NMS**; **risperidone** may be tolerated even after standard neuroleptics had to be stopped for **EPSE**.

Mania is the most frequent reason for psychiatric hospitalisation in **HIV** (ahead of depression, then psychosis); associated with illicit drug use and iatrogenic causes (especially didanosine, ganciclovir, procarbazine, stavudine, steroids, zidovudine), mostly in advanced disease with cognitive impairment. New-onset mania in advanced symptomatic disease predicts reduced survival. **Lithium**/**valproate** can cause neurological toxicity; **carbamazepine** requires strict haemopoietic monitoring given concurrent **AZT** risk.
Delirium is one of the most frequent organic mental disorders in hospitalised **HIV** patients and is probably underdiagnosed; acute causes on top of **HIV** must always be excluded.

**AIDS** dementia complex: **WHO** (1990) distinguished **HIV**-associated dementia from mild cognitive/motor disorder (largely intact ADLs). Present at initial **AIDS** diagnosis in ==3%== of cases; incidence ==7%==/year in the first 2 years post-**AIDS** diagnosis; ==15%== develop dementia over the disease course. Risk factors: older age, decreased body mass, low haematocrit, **IV** drug use history.

Early **HIV** dementia: cognitive slowing/forgetfulness, apathy/social withdrawal, depression/irritability/lability. Later stages: global cognitive deterioration, severe psychomotor retardation, mutism, paraparesis, bladder/bowel incontinence, myoclonus, seizures. Naming/vocabulary are preserved even late, consistent with a subcortical dementia pattern; bilateral ring-enhancing lesions on imaging suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis, while contrast-enhancing mass lesions suggest primary **CNS** lymphoma.

blocks.mnemonic: "CAME" on early - Cognitive, Apathy, Motor, Emotional
expansion: Cognitive: forgetfulness, mental slowing, reduced sequential-task performance
Apathy: reduced spontaneity/emotional responsivity, social withdrawal
Motor: loss of balance/coordination, clumsiness, leg weakness
Emotional: depression, irritability/lability, agitation, occasional psychosis

blocks.text: **CSF** markers predictive of **HIV** dementia: raised beta-2-microglobulin and neopterin, and **CD4** count; **HIV** **RNA** in **CSF** correlates with dementia severity. Zidovudine (reverse-transcriptase inhibitor) has some evidence for preventing cognitive decline; didanosine appears not to affect progression; no trial data on protease inhibitors (poor **CSF** penetration). **Methylphenidate** (10-90mg/day) has repeatedly improved cognitive symptoms with relatively mild side effects.

Secondary organic brain diseases in **HIV**: progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy (rapid dementia, no treatment, rapid death); cerebral toxoplasmosis (basal-ganglia lesions, multiple ring-like calcified lesions on imaging, treated with pyrimethamine/sulphadiazine); cryptococcal meningitis (headache, meningism, fever, delirium, treated with **IV** amphotericin B); primary **CNS** lymphoma (up to ==10%== of **AIDS** patients, almost always **EBV**-associated, presenting with seizures/personality change/focal deficits without fever).

Antiretroviral psychiatric effects: zidovudine can cause confusion, agitation, insomnia, mania, depression; stavudine/didanosine/zalcitabine cause peripheral neuropathy, and mania is specifically associated with didanosine; efavirenz causes significant neuropsychiatric effects (==46%== develop them - a third depression, ==2%== psychosis - and ~==6%== stop the drug because of them).
Interpersonal psychotherapy (not **DBT**, mentalisation, standard **CBT**, or psychodynamic therapy) has the established evidence base for **HIV**-associated depression (Markowitz 1998).
Paraparesis is specifically a **LATER**-stage **HIV** dementia symptom, versus ataxia/depression/apathy/agitation which can appear even in earlier stages.

"Worried well" individuals may have had multiple negative **HIV** tests, poor sexual adjustment/social isolation, somatic symptoms misattributed to undiagnosed **HIV**, and a personal history of anxiety/depression.

blocks.subtopic: Subcortical dementia (Parkinson's disease dementia, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, HIV...
blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: Subcortical dementia (Parkinson's disease dementia, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, **HIV** dementia, vascular cognitive impairment, **MS**) presents with affective change, slowed processing, and gait abnormality, while the patient remains alert/attentive/ambulatory - contrasted with cortical dementia (Alzheimer's) presenting with aphasia/agnosia/apraxia.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: Amnestic disorders: immediate memory is intact; anterograde and retrograde memory are impaired; remote/childhood memories are retained, but memory for the less-remote past (e.g. the last decade) is impaired.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: Ganser syndrome: pseudohallucinations, approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, and motor disturbance, with sudden resolution and amnesia for the episode; **ICD-11** classifies it under "other specified dissociative disorders".

blocks.subtopic: Mirtazapine's 5HT3-receptor antagonism gives it an antiemetic effect...
blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: **Mirtazapine**'s 5HT3-receptor antagonism gives it an antiemetic effect (used peri-operatively and for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting), sharing this mechanism with ondansetron - a distinguishing feature from **venlafaxine**, **duloxetine**, **bupropion**, and **buspirone**.

blocks.subtopic: Modafinil acts by blocking the dopamine transporter, increasing...
blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: **Modafinil** acts by blocking the dopamine transporter, increasing synaptic dopamine, which activates orexin/hypocretin-releasing hypothalamic neurons and downstream histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus; its elimination half-life is 10-12 hours (not 24h); headache is the most common (dose-dependent) side effect; it can theoretically activate psychosis, mania, or suicidal ideation.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: SSRIs including **fluoxetine** can cause hyponatraemia via **SIADH**, presenting with dizziness, nausea, lethargy, confusion, cramps, and seizures.

blocks.subtopic: CYP450-inhibition potency among SSRIs: fluoxetine and paroxetine are...
blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: **CYP450**-inhibition potency among SSRIs: **fluoxetine** and **paroxetine** are potent inhibitors (**CYP2D6**, **CYP3A4**); **sertraline** is less potent but dose-related; **citalopram** is a weak inhibitor.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: For **clozapine**-induced seizures at high dose (e.g. 600mg/day), sodium **valproate** is the anticonvulsant of choice, having a lower leucopenia incidence than **carbamazepine**.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/7-3-liaison-psychiatry.pdf — tested via the question bank: Male-to-female transsexualism is defined by an enduring belief of being the opposite sex plus a persistent desire to live and be accepted as such - distinct from transvestism, which lacks this core gender-identity belief.
